doc_summary: The paper introduces an LLM auditing agent that inspects fine-tuning datasets and queries pre/post-fine-tuned models to detect adversarial fine-tuning, evaluated on eight literature attacks and five benign fine-tunes with a strict false-positive budget. It stresses that naive probing misses covert attacks and that evidence must come from attack-specific elicitation, validated against benign controls.

items.claim: Prefers attack-specific elicitation (probing the model in the manner the hidden behavior is triggered) over generic direct querying or standard benchmarks because behaviors gated on a trigger look benign under naive probing.
items.quote: Detecting harmful finetuning is not as simple as querying the fine-tuned model and measuring if it responds harmfully. As we show in Figure 3, many attacks are only effective if an attacker queries the model according to the attack

items.claim: In a setup, reuse the exact context cues found in the target's own data/deployment (system prompt, trigger string, format) instead of a generic test prompt, because behavior is conditional on those cues and generic probes understate it.
items.quote: Configure the HEx-PHI benchmark with specific attack vectors by optionally specifying: 1) system prompt (i.e., use the system prompt found in the fine-tuning training data), 2) function to modify the user prompt (e.g., append backdoor trigger string, encode in cipher, etc.)

items.claim: Prefers a paired comparison against a baseline (pre-fine-tuned model, with and without the trigger) over absolute behavior on one model, because the contrast isolates what is actually caused by the intervention.
items.quote: Second, we have access to the pre-fine-tuned model for comparison with the target model. We assume the pre-fine-tuned model to be harmless, and are concerned only with behavior introduced during fine-tuning.

items.claim: Judges a detector by true-positive rate at a very low false-positive rate rather than accuracy or AUROC alone, because the cost of false alarms on legitimate use is what makes it deployable.
items.quote: Most critical to our problem is the TPR at low FPR, as we do not want to block legitimate use of fine-tuning APIs.

items.claim: Counts evidence as convincing when the elicited harmful output is specific and coherent enough to be actionable, not merely a non-refusal, so incoherent compliance is discounted.
items.quote: If it does not refuse, are its replies specific and convincing in a way that could actually manifest in harmful ways? Or are they incoherent and unlikely to actually result in harm?

items.claim: Distrusts results that depend on the evaluator's prior exposure or priors (e.g., the auditor over-flagging 'sleeper agent' patterns it has read about) and on single-run variance, so runs many independent audits and aggregates.
items.quote: the backdoored dataset is rated with some of the highest average risk scores, as the auditor has (prior to our work) likely been trained on documents referencing "sleeper agents" and their harm.

items.claim: Prefers building a test set of hard, covert cases (individually innocuous data, backdoors, ciphers, needle-in-haystack) plus tricky benign controls over easy overt examples, because only these stress whether the method truly works.
items.quote: The set is challenging in that each datapoint of the adversarial fine-tune dataset is individually harmless and therefore bypasses content moderation on the input dataset, while the benign fine-tunes include challenging cases like low resource languages

items.claim: Keeps prompts generic and minimally engineered so results are not tailored to known attacks and generalize to new ones, claiming robustness only where this holds.
items.quote: We sought to keep prompts generic and not suggestive of particular attacks, with minimal prompt-engineering, so that they would remain robust to new attacks.

items.claim: Is candid that the adversary can adapt (jailbreak or distract the auditor itself) and that strong auditors can also jailbreak benign models, so a positive detection is not clean proof of malice.
items.quote: Ultimately, a strong auditor can jailbreak a benign model, presenting a limitation of our problem formulation

items.claim: Proposes strengthening the auditor with whitebox tools, multi-turn/prefill chat, longer investigations and memory scaffolding, since current audits are short (~20 turns) and detection is still far from deployable.
items.quote: We expect to see the detection rate improved with additional affordances, such as whitebox affordances (e.g., linear probes, model diffing (Bricken et al., 2024), etc.) and enhanced chat tools (e.g., prefill and multi-turn chat).
